newsitem.title: UK: Morgan Grenfell under pressure as redemptions mount.
newsitem.headline: Morgan Grenfell under pressure as redemptions mount.

text.p: Morgan Grenfell came under pressure on Tuesday to confirm it has a contingency plan in place to cover further withdrawals from its beleaguered investment funds as redemptions continued.

But Morgan Grenfell Asset management, the fund management arm of German banking giant Deutsche Bank AG, took some comfort from the fact that Tuesday's redemptions amounted to some 24 million pounds ($37.29 million), down from Monday's 39 million pounds.

But the new figure moved the total to just over 250 million pounds and ever nearer exhausting the 300 million pounds pile of cash the firm has in place to cover withdrawals following last week's temporary suspension of the funds.

The suspension followed the disclosure that there had been irregularities in the way they have been run and led to two fund managers being suspended and a full-scale regulatory investigation being launched.

In Frankfurt, Deutsche shares closed 39 pfennigs lower at 71.50 marks, above earlier lows, with sentiment hit by news that the bank's precious triple-A credit rating was under examination by Moody's Investor Service, one of the most influential debt rating organisations in the market.

Banking analysts continued to cut their 1996 earnings forecasts for Deutsche with Konrad Becker at Merck, Finck pruning his estimate to 4.5 marks from 5.0 but maintaining his buy recommendation on the stock.

In London, Morgan Grenfell would neither confirm or deny the existence of a plan to raise extra cash but industry sources said the money is likely to be in place already in order to satisfy regulators that continuing investor demand for redemptions will be met.
"It's inconceivable that Deutsche hasn't made a plan just in case they need to top up the amount of money they have available," said one senior source.

The current 300 million pounds cushion is made up of the 180 million pounds Deutsche pumped into the funds last week by removing some of the unlisted stocks which were the original cause of the problems and cash which was already present.
MGAM has three options available to raise further cash.
There could be another plain injection of money by Deutsche which would probably be the simplest way out but might have wider repercussions for the German banking giant.

Analysts have already started to prune their earnings forecasts for 1995 and credit rating agency Moody's has said it is looking at the bank's coveted triple-A rating in the light of what has been going on at MGAM.

MGAM could also sell some of the contents of the funds but this could be a painful experience given the lack of liquidity in some of the investments and the fact that, as a distressed seller, MGAM's market competitors will play hard ball.
The third alternative looks the most likely.
With permission from fund trustees, Royal Bank of Scotland, MGAM would be able to borrow 10 percent of the value of the funds from its wealthy parent in order to finance redemptions.
It is likely that Deutsche would prefer this route because it could be paid back from the fund when the dust has settled.

The bank's previous 180 million pounds injection has not disappeared down a black hole but it is almost impossible to estimate what the securities, which have a high proportion of speculative high-tech unlisted stocks, will be worth when they have been properly valued.
